edits.text:
Tuberous sclerosis Skin — ash-leaf (hypopigmented) spots, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood · Brain — calcified subependymal nodules along the ventricles on CT, and cortical tubers, better seen on MRI; epilepsy in most, often beginning as infantile spasms, though a first seizure can come at any age; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders · Growth to watch — a subependymal nodule can enlarge into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that blocks CSF outflow; the resulting obstructive hydrocephalus needs resection · Heart and kidney — cardiac rhabdomyomas; renal angiomyolipomas · Diagnosis — the clinical constellation, genetic testing, or both · Surveillance — skin and eye examinations, serial brain and kidney MRI, a baseline echocardiogram with serial ECGs, a baseline EEG, and neuropsychiatric screening
Tuberous sclerosis versus its mimics Neurofibromatosis type 1 — also autosomal dominant with seizures, but the skin lesions are pigmented café-au-lait macules and cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk, with optic gliomas; a hypopigmented spot or a nail-fold fibroma is not NF1 · Von Hippel-Lindau — autosomal dominant, but its tumors are cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, with no characteristic skin lesion · Ataxia-telangiectasia — autosomal recessive; childhood ataxia, oculomotor problems and telangiectasias, not hamartomas · Infective endocarditis — fever, dyspnea and a murmur; its nail finding is a splinter hemorrhage under the nail, not a fibroma growing from the nail fold
